12988-representative-plays-by-american-d:
This volume of Representative Plays by American Dramatists presents Augustus Thomas's In Mizzoura, a play in four acts. An introduction on play prefaces argues that authors' own remarks reveal attitude and technical purpose better than press agents. Schiller on The Robbers and Hugo on Cromwell and Hernani serve as examples. American dramatists, it laments, rarely left such self-examination.

Inside the play, Bollinger and Joe trade Missouri dialect about Sam Fowler. He is held prisoner by an express company and living on the fat of the land, while friends gather testimony for false imprisonment damages. Thomas writes with local colour and humour. The volume preserves a popular American stage work of its era.
8736-gaspar-ruiz:
Joseph Conrad opens Gaspar Ruiz with a reflection on revolutionary war, which raises strange characters out of the obscurity of humble lives. Most such figures grow famous briefly through vice, virtue, or action, then are forgotten, while only a few leaders survive in books. General Santierra, a South American of good family counted among the liberators from Spanish rule, attained that cold, paper-and-ink immortality Conrad describes.

Against that backdrop, the novella follows Gaspar Ruiz himself, a strong, simple man swept into war, love, and betrayal on the Chilean frontier. Conrad's narrator pieces the story together from Santierra's account, giving it the feel of recovered history. The tale's power lies in its portrait of a man too large and too loyal for the causes that use him. Readers new to Conrad will find a shorter, more direct entry to his world than the great novels.
britannica-1911-abd-ul-aziz:
Abd-ul-Aziz receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abd-ul-Aziz, sultan of Turkey, was born in 1830 and succeeded his brother Abd-ul-Mejid in 1861. State loans of his reign fed his purse, the entry charges, through palace building and sharp dealing in the debt.

Egypt's khedive paid hard cash for firmans that widened his house's rights. The sultan toured Europe in 1867, first of his line to do so, and took the Garter from Queen Victoria. Suez Canal guests crowded his court in 1869. Misrule, empty coffers, and the Bulgarian atrocities brought deposition in May 1876, hailed with joy, the entry states. A fortnight later he was found dead, by suicide on the medical word.
britannica-1911-aguilera-ventura-ruiz:
Aguilera, Ventura Ruiz, a Spanish poet of 1820 to 1881, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Salamanca, he graduated there in medicine, then moved to Madrid in 1844 and turned to journalism. A collection of poems, Ecos nacionales, won him wide popularity in 1849. He later directed the national archaeological museum at Madrid.

His Elegias y Armonias of 1863 matched the success of his first collection. Later books, the Satiras and Estaciones del ano, showed his powers fading, in the entry's judgement. Aguilera wrote under Lamartine's clear influence, preaching liberalism and Christianity in verse. The poems lacked force, the entry allows, but they leave a strong sense of sincere devotion and a charming personality behind the lines.
britannica-1911-greiz:
Greiz is a town of Germany, capital of the principality of Reuss-Greiz, in a pleasant valley on the right bank of the White Elster, 66 miles by rail south of Leipzig. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 23,114 people in 1905, nearly double its 1875 figure. Old town and new town face each other across the river.

The prince's palace in its park, the old chateau on its rocky hill, and the old town church of 1225 head the entry's list of buildings. Statues of William I and of Bismarck stand in the town. Its industries are considerable: dyeing, tanning, and woollen, cotton, shawl, coverlet and paper making, with a school of textile industry. The entry calls Greiz apparently a town of Slav origin. Fire destroyed it wholly in 1494 and almost wholly in 1802.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cadiz:
Cadiz is a diocese under Seville covering nearly all of the Spanish province of Cadiz, with its bishop living in the city of Cadiz on the Isle of Leon. The old town largely burned in 1569, and the city, retaken from the Moors in 1262, was raised to a see in 1263 by Urban IV, acting at Alfonso X's request. Its first bishop was Friar Juan Martinez.

After Algeciras fell to the Christians, the bishops of Cadiz also bore the title of Algeciras, granted by Clement VI in 1352. Among its prelates was Cardinal Juan de Torquemada in 1441, a Dominican theologian who took a leading part at Basle and Florence. By the Concordat of 1851 the suppressed diocese of Ceuta joined Cadiz, which counts 32 parishes and 110 priests, with 22 parishes in Ceuta.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-von-milt:
Karl von Miltiz, papal chamberlain and nuncio, was born about 1480, son of Sigismund von Miltiz, and drowned in the Main in 1529. Educated at Mainz, Trier, and Meissen, he went to Rome in 1514 or 1515 and became papal chamberlain and notary. He acted as agent for Frederick, Elector of Saxony, and Duke George the Bearded. For the duke he obtained leave to carry Campo Santo earth from Rome to Annaberg's cemetery.

After Cardinal Cajetan failed to silence Luther, Miltiz seemed the man to bring negotiations to a good end. His pretext for Germany was delivering the coveted papal golden rose to his elector. At Altenburg he first talked with Luther; they agreed to keep silent, leaving examination to Archbishop Richard of Trier. At Leipzig he heaped mortifying, unnecessary reproaches on Tetzel. But the movement had gone too far, and further meetings at Liebenwerda in 1519 and Lichtenburg in 1520 came to nothing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-markus-hansiz:
Markus Hansiz was a historian, born at Volkermarkt in Carinthia in 1683 and dead at Vienna in 1766. He joined the Jesuits at fifteen at Eberndorf, was ordained in 1708, and taught humanities at Vienna. From 1713 to 1717 he taught philosophy at Graz, then gave himself wholly to history.

Models such as Wharton's Anglia Sacra and Ughelli's Italia Sacra, plus librarian Bernardo Gentilotti's counsel, set him on a vast Germania Sacra. He scoured libraries and archives, publishing in 1727 to 1729 histories of Lorch church and the sees of Passau and Salzburg. He gathered material for Ratisbon, Vienna, Neustadt, Seckau, Gurk, and Lavant dioceses and Carinthia's secular history, but published only a preliminary Ratisbon inquiry in 1754. He clashed with Salzburg tradition by dating St Rupert's founding of that see to the late seventh century, and with St Emmeram's canons over his third volume, emerging with honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-aviz:
The Order of Aviz, a Portuguese military order, fought the Moors under perpetual vows where crusaders' temporary vows ran out. Templars reached Portugal by 1128, and a native order arose about 1146, first called Brothers of Santa Maria of Évora after Afonso gave them that captured town.

Pedro Henriquez served as first grand master, and after the castle of Aviz fell, the knights took its name and Benedict's rule as shaped by Cistercians in 1162. Like Calatrava's knights, they held border castles, farmed estates, and fought through the Reconquest into modern honorary form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-system-of-lei:
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, born at Leipzig in June 1646, was a philosopher, mathematician, diplomat, and historian in one life. He studied philosophy and law at Leipzig and took his law doctorate at Altdorf in 1666. He served the Elector of Mainz and spent 1672 to 1676 at Louis XIV's court, with a London visit among England's leading scholars. In 1676 he became librarian and councillor to Brunswick, and died at Hanover in 1716.

With Newton he shares credit for inventing differential calculus in 1675, and he prized observation over speculation, documents over theory, and comparison of languages. As a thinker on statecraft he pressed freedom of conscience with persistence. The entry then sets out his philosophical system, judging him, like Plato, by the loftiness of his thought rather than by scientific precision.
doe-osti-17197666-complete-the-microstru:
Jian Chen, Roger Miller, and Zhili Feng of Oak Ridge finish characterizing laser welds in irradiated nickel alloy 182, in a September 2025 report for the Light Water Reactor Sustainability Program. Repair welding on reactor parts grows hard as neutron exposure builds helium inside the metal: even tiny helium amounts can crack a hot weld. Alloy 182 held helium up to 20 atomic parts per million in these tests.

Samples from the fiscal 2024 weld campaign at the Radiochemical Engineering Development Center were laser welded in a hot cell with refined settings. Microscopy then mapped the weld microstructure and any cracking. The milestone work, done with the Electric Power Research Institute, moves the industry toward validated repair methods for extending plant life past 60 years.
doe-osti-3003003-simulating-isotropic-ra:
David J. Miller, Elizabeth M. Berg, and Leiph A. Preston simulate earthquake waves in Sandia report SAND2025-13849, printed November 2025. The site is Rock Valley, a test area used for seismic research. The team computes horizontal-to-vertical ratios for Rayleigh waves, the rolling surface waves that dominate many seismograms. The ratio carries information about the ground structure beneath a station.

Two methods are compared. A one-dimensional calculation gives a quick estimate from a layered ground model. Full three-dimensional waveform simulations then test that estimate against a detailed velocity model. Synthetic seismograms from several source positions feed the comparison. Matching the two tells seismologists when the cheap method suffices. The work supports monitoring programs that read ground structure from sparse stations at test sites.
doe-osti-3014498-toward-a-microscopic-pi:
Felix Ringer of Old Dominion University wrote this final technical report for award DE-SC0024358. It covers July 2023 to August 2024. The topic is hadronization and multi-parton processes. When quarks and gluons are produced in collider collisions, they must dress themselves into the color-neutral hadrons detectors see. That last step is hadronization. It happens at low energies, where QCD calculations are hardest. It anchors this theory project.

The report situates the work among RHIC, the LHC, and Jefferson Lab's CEBAF. The coming Electron-Ion Collider is part of the picture too. Factorization separates the hard scattering, the parton shower, and hadronization into treatable pieces. The project pushed on the third piece. Much of the narrative is training. Graduate students attended the HUGS summer school and a Jefferson Lab quantum computing bootcamp. Two Research Experiences for Undergraduates students were supervised at ODU and Jefferson Lab.
doe-osti-3399496-un-synthesis-fabricatio: UN got LEU-synthesized, and this DOE text covers uranium nitride fabrication. The pages detail the oxidation findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The fuel was advanced. The data were nuclear. The UC were study. The advanced were fuel.
gaspar-ruiz:
Joseph Conrad sets Gaspar Ruiz in South America in the years of the wars for freedom from Spain. Gaspar is a strong, simple soldier, pressed into service and then falsely marked as a deserter. He suffers harsh use from both sides and lacks the sharp mind to weigh treason. A young officer who served under General Robles tells his story years later.

Ruiz escapes, joins the royalist side, and rises by sheer strength and nerve. A letter thrust into a sentry's hand brings him back into the patriot camp's plans. Conrad uses the tale to probe fate, pride, and how war bends a plain man. The prose is slow, grave, and full of dry humor about the men who command.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAOrganization:
Three organizational charts map the Central Intelligence Agency at three moments: 1950, 1961, and 1963. Each chart lays out the agency's directorates, offices, and chains of command as they stood in that year, in the CIA's own diagramming.

Read in sequence, the charts show a young agency hardening into a bureaucracy. New offices appear, the clandestine service takes shape, and the structure of 1963 stands on the eve of the Kennedy assassination. Org charts are dry documents, but for intelligence historians they are skeleton keys, fixing who reported to whom when it mattered. The three charts are filed as released, a reference set.
representative-plays-by-american-dramati:
In Mizzoura, a play in four acts by Augustus Thomas, appears in this set of representative American plays with an essay on its making. Thomas was born at St. Louis, Missouri, on January 8, 1859. The essay begins with the value of dramatists' own prefaces, citing Schiller and Victor Hugo as models.

American playwrights, it laments, seldom left such accounts of their work, and their letters went unkept. Samuel French's edition of Thomas's works repairs that loss: the playwright wrote reminiscent accounts of six plays. His own account of how In Mizzoura grew is used here, sparing the editor long comment of his own.
